'''Uketa Shrine''' (うけたじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} in Hozu-chō Tateiwa, {{ill|Kameoka, Kyoto|Q633996|qid=Q633996}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|Q120730|qid=Q120730}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} {{ill|Shikinai Ronsha|Q135022904|qid=Q135022904}}.

It stands in eastern {{ill|Kameoka, Kyoto|Q633996|qid=Q633996}}, at the entrance to {{ill|Hozu Gorge|Q10887680|qid=Q10887680}}, where the river's name changes from "{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōi River}}" to "{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hozu River}}." Across the river stands {{ill|Kuwada Shrine|Q11537594|qid=Q11537594|lt=Kuwata Shrine}}. Together with Kuwata Shrine, it is connected with traditions about the excavation of Hozu Gorge.

=== Enshrined deities ===
* {{ill|Oyamakui no Kami|ja|大山咋神|simple|Oyamakui no Kami|zh|大山咋神|qid=Q10935105|lt=Ōyamakui-no-Kami}} (おおやまくいのかみ)
* {{ill|Ichikishima-hime|Q11059454|qid=Q11059454|qid=Q11059454|lt=Ichikishimahime-no-Mikoto}} (いちきしまひめのみこと) - also called Sayorihime-no-Mikoto.

=== History ===
Because shrine buildings and documents were destroyed by military fire in the {{ill|Eiroku|Q1143341|qid=Q1143341}} era ({{ill|1558|Q6601|qid=Q6601}}-{{ill|1570|Q6659|qid=Q6659}}), detailed origins are unclear<ref name=setsumei>Explanatory board in the precincts.</ref>. The enshrined deity Ōyamakui-no-Kami is said to be a deity who came from Izumo to develop the Tanba region, then a lake area, and to have begun excavating Hozu Gorge from the site of {{ill|Kuwada Shrine|Q11537594|qid=Q11537594}} opposite Uketa Shrine<ref name=setsumei/>. It is said the shrine name "Uketa" comes from accepting (uketa) this groundbreaking hoe-rite for that development<ref name=setsumei/>. Traditions that the Kameoka Basin was once a lake remain in many nearby places (see "{{ill|Kameoka Basin|Q11181997|qid=Q11181997}}" for details).

Shrine tradition gives its foundation as {{ill|Wadō (era)|Q1373026|qid=Q1373026}} 2 ({{ill|709|Q23514|qid=Q23514}}). Because the shrine site was called "Iwao," it is identified as a {{ill|Shikinai Ronsha|Q135022904|qid=Q135022904}} for the {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} listed in the mid-{{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}} {{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}} {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}} as "Ishio Shrine" in {{ill|Kuwada district|Q11537600|qid=Q11537600}}, {{ill|Tanba Province|cs|Tanba (provincie)|de|Provinz Tamba|es|Provincia de Tanba|fa|ولایت تانبا|fr|Province de Tanba|gl|Provincia de Tanba|id|Provinsi Tamba|it|Tanba (provincia)|ja|丹波国|ko|단바국|lt|Tambos žemė|nl|Tamba (provincie)|pt|Província de Tanba|ru|Тамба (провинция)|simple|Tamba Province|sk|Tanba (provincia)|sr|Провинција Тамба|tr|Tamba (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Тамба|zh|丹波國|zh_min_nan|Tanba-kok|qid=Q954511}}. For unclear reasons, there is also a theory identifying it as Matsuo Shrine, another shikinaisha of Kuwata District<ref>Other candidate shrines for Matsuo Shrine include {{ill|Matsuo Shrine (Kameoka)|Q11529679|qid=Q11529679|lt=Matsuo Shrine}} in Asahi-chō, Kameoka.</ref>.

After the destruction by fire in the Eiroku era, it was moved to Miyanoue (present Hozu Hachimangū)<ref name=chimei>''Place Names of Kyoto Prefecture'', entry for Hozu village.</ref>. It returned to the current site in the {{ill|Kan'ei|Q1192913|qid=Q1192913}} era ({{ill|1624|Q6821|qid=Q6821}}-{{ill|1645|Q6925|qid=Q6925}})<ref name=chimei/>, but at Miyanoue a divided spirit is still enshrined as a {{ill|tongū|Q11664877|qid=Q11664877}}.

In the early modern period, Hozu Gorge was called "Uketa Gorge," and with Uketa Shrine, the Kuwata Shrine on the opposite bank was also called "Uketa Shrine" or "Uketa Shrine (floating-field shrine)."

=== Subsidiary shrines ===
'''Precinct sub-shrine'''
* Inari Shrine - located beside the honden.

'''Off-site shrine'''
[[File:Hozu-hachimangū keidai.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Hozu Hachimangū precincts}}{{small|Hachimangū at back left; Uketa Shrine {{ill|tongū|Q11664877|qid=Q11664877}} at right. Both are Kyoto Prefecture designated cultural properties.}}]]
* {{ill|Tongū|Q11664877|qid=Q11664877}}
*: Located in the precincts of Hozu Hachimangū (21 Miyanoue, Hozu-chō, Kameoka). Uketa Shrine is said to have been temporarily moved here from the Eiroku era to the Kan'ei era, and after returning, a divided spirit continued to be enshrined here as a tongū ({{ill|Otabisho|Q11489117|qid=Q11489117}}). Its style is one-bay {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684|qid=Q210684}}. Hachimangū is said to have drifted here from Hosokawa village in Kita-Kuwata District during the Kan'ei era and was rebuilt on the former Uketa Shrine site after Uketa's return<ref name=chimei/>. On the hill to the north remains a bell tower as a relic of Wakōin, the former shrine-temple (now abolished){{ill|Jingū-ji|Q1074971|qid=Q1074971}}. These three structures, Hozu Hachimangū's honden and bell tower and Uketa Shrine's tongū, are designated cultural properties of Kyoto Prefecture<ref name="教育委員会">[http://www.kyoto-be.ne.jp/bunkazai/cms/?page_id=200 Kyoto Prefecture designated/registered cultural properties] (Kyoto Prefectural Board of Education).</ref><ref>[https://www.city.kameoka.kyoto.jp/shakai/bunkazai/hozuhachiman-uketa.html New Kyoto Prefecture cultural-property designation for Kameoka cultural assets] (Kameoka City website).</ref>.

=== Festivals ===
* Autumn Grand Festival ({{ill|October 21|Q2960|qid=Q2960}})
*: Also called the "Hozu Fire Festival." It begins with the eve festival; the divine spirit is welcomed from the main sanctuary to the tongū within Hozu Hachimangū.
